lead: This unit explains how light is guided inside an optical fiber and how guided light is described at three levels: rays, modes and periodic structures. After it you can compute acceptance angle, numerical aperture, V number and cutoff wavelength, and read the basic diagrams of fiber, integrated waveguide and photonic crystal devices.
about: This unit builds the physical picture of light in an optical fiber. Chapter 1.1 lays out the complete link and why fiber beats copper. Chapter 1.2 uses rays and total internal reflection to find the critical and acceptance angles, and Chapter 1.3 turns them into the numerical aperture, the relative index difference and the wider acceptance of skew rays. Chapter 1.4 replaces rays with electromagnetic modes in a planar guide. Chapters 1.5 and 1.6 apply the mode picture to step-index, graded-index, single-mode and multimode fibers: the V number, the mode count and the cutoff wavelength. Chapter 1.7 separates phase velocity from the group velocity that sets pulse delay. Chapter 1.8 moves the same confinement onto a chip as strip and channel waveguides, and Chapter 1.9 ends with photonic crystals and the photonic band gap.

chapters.idea: An optical fiber link moves information as light: electrical signal to light source, through fiber, then photodetector back to electrical signal.
chapters.depth: Block diagram of the general system: transmitter, fiber channel, receiver. Define source, fiber, photodetector. List advantages over copper: wide bandwidth, low loss, immunity to electromagnetic interference, small size, electrical isolation and security. Mention common wavelength windows 850 nm, 1300 nm and 1550 nm only as names; leave loss values to Unit 2. Include analog and digital links at block level.
chapters.example: A 20 km fiber link uses a 1550 nm source and has fiber loss 0.2 dB/km. Find the total fiber loss. If the input power is 1 mW, find the output power in mW. Total loss = 20 km × 0.2 dB/km = 4 dB. Input 1 mW is 0 dBm, so output is −4 dBm. Output power = 1 mW × 10^(−4/10) = 0.398 mW, about 0.4 mW.
chapters.trap: Loss in dB adds over distance. Do not treat 0.2 dB/km as total loss, and do not multiply powers in dB; add dB values.
chapters.leave: Leave attenuation mechanisms to Unit 2, source structures to Unit 3 and detector structures to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Light stays in the core by total internal reflection when it strikes the core–cladding boundary above the critical angle; this sets an acceptance cone at the input.
chapters.depth: Refractive index, Snell's law, critical angle θc = sin⁻¹(n2/n1), total internal reflection, meridional ray, acceptance angle θa. Derive for a step-index fiber with air outside: sin θa = √(n1² − n2²) when n0 = 1. Define n0, n1 and n2. Explain that the ray must go from denser core to rarer cladding and must exceed θc. Mention numerical aperture only as sin θa; leave full treatment to Chapter 1.3.
chapters.example: A step-index fiber has core index n1 = 1.50 and cladding index n2 = 1.45. The outside medium is air, n0 = 1. Find the critical angle and the acceptance angle. θc = sin⁻¹(1.45/1.50) = 75.2°. NA = √(1.50² − 1.45²) = √(2.25 − 2.1025) = 0.384. θa = sin⁻¹(0.384) = 22.6°.
chapters.trap: Use n2/n1 for the critical angle, not n1/n2. The acceptance angle is measured in air outside the fiber, not inside the core.
chapters.leave: Leave numerical aperture details and skew rays to Chapter 1.3; leave electromagnetic modes to Chapter 1.4.

chapters.idea: Numerical aperture measures the light-gathering cone; skew rays travel helically and need a modified bound-ray condition.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in detail. Define NA = sin θa = √(n1² − n2²) for air, and divide by n0 for a general outside medium. Relate NA to relative index difference Δ: NA ≈ n1√(2Δ). Define meridional rays, which cross the axis, and skew rays, which do not. State that skew rays follow helical paths and the simple meridional acceptance angle does not fully describe them. Keep mathematics short.
chapters.trap: NA is dimensionless. θa is an angle in air; it is not the angle inside the core. Skew rays are not covered by the simple meridional acceptance formula.
chapters.leave: Leave exact skew-ray acceptance calculations to advanced texts and leave dispersion to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Maxwell's equations in a layered dielectric give only discrete field patterns, called modes, that can travel without changing shape in a planar guide.
chapters.depth: Electromagnetic wave equation, boundary conditions for tangential E and H, transverse resonance in a slab. Define planar guide, core, cladding, TE and TM modes. Introduce mode number m and field profile. Define V = (2πd/λ)√(n1² − n2²) for a symmetric planar guide of thickness d. State that guided modes occur when V > mπ, giving about floor(V/π) + 1 modes. Mention cylindrical fiber only as the next step; leave LP mode labels to Chapter 1.6.
chapters.example: A symmetric planar guide has n1 = 1.50, n2 = 1.48, core thickness d = 5 µm and wavelength λ = 1.3 µm. Find V and the number of guided modes. √(1.50² − 1.48²) = √(2.25 − 2.1904) = 0.2441. V = (2π × 5/1.3) × 0.2441 = 24.166 × 0.2441 = 5.90. Number of modes = floor(5.90/π) + 1 = floor(1.88) + 1 = 2.
chapters.trap: For a planar guide use core thickness d in V. For a cylindrical fiber the V formula uses core radius a. Do not mix the two formulas.
chapters.leave: Leave cylindrical LP modes to Chapter 1.6, and leave attenuation and dispersion to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Step-index fiber has a sudden core–cladding index jump; graded-index fiber smooths the index to reduce modal dispersion.
chapters.depth: Fiber structure: core, cladding and protective jacket. Define step-index and graded-index profiles. For graded index use n(r) = n1[1 − 2Δ(r/a)^α]^(1/2) for r < a, with core radius a and profile parameter α. Define Δ ≈ (n1 − n2)/n1. Give NA = √(n1² − n2²). Compare ray paths: straight zig-zag in step-index, curved path in graded-index. Mention parabolic graded index α = 2. Keep cylindrical geometry as context, not full mode theory.
chapters.example: A step-index fiber has n1 = 1.48, n2 = 1.46, core radius a = 25 µm and λ = 1.30 µm. Find Δ, NA, V and the approximate number of modes. Δ ≈ (1.48 − 1.46)/1.48 = 0.0135. NA = √(1.48² − 1.46²) = 0.2425. V = (2π × 25/1.30) × 0.2425 = 120.83 × 0.2425 = 29.3. V > 2.405, so it is multimode. Number of modes ≈ V²/2 = 429.
chapters.trap: V uses core radius a, not core diameter. Δ has an exact definition with squares and an approximate definition with n1 − n2; say which one you use.
chapters.leave: Leave modal dispersion and attenuation mechanisms to Unit 2, and leave single-mode cutoff to Chapter 1.6.

chapters.idea: A fiber is single-mode only above a cutoff wavelength; below it, several modes travel and interfere.
chapters.depth: Single-mode and multimode fibers. Define V = (2πa/λ)NA for a cylindrical step-index fiber. State the single-mode condition V < 2.405. Derive cutoff wavelength λc = 2πa NA/2.405. Explain that λ > λc gives single-mode operation. Mention mode field diameter and the practical advantage of single-mode fiber for long links. Compare with multimode step-index and graded-index fibers at block level.
chapters.example: A step-index fiber has core radius a = 4 µm and NA = 0.11. Find the cutoff wavelength. At λ = 1.31 µm, is it single-mode? λc = 2πa NA/2.405 = (2π × 4 × 0.11)/2.405 = 2.7646/2.405 = 1.15 µm. At 1.31 µm, V = 2.7646/1.31 = 2.11. Since 2.11 < 2.405, the fiber is single-mode at 1.31 µm.
chapters.trap: Single-mode means λ is longer than λc, so V is smaller than 2.405. Do not call wavelengths shorter than λc single-mode.
chapters.leave: Leave chromatic and polarization-mode dispersion to Unit 2, and source launching to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A light wave has a phase velocity for its crests and a group velocity for its pulse envelope; signal timing follows group velocity.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in detail. Define phase velocity vp = ω/β = c/n_eff. Define group velocity vg = dω/dβ = c/N_g. Define group index N_g = n_eff − λ dn_eff/dλ. Explain that a pulse carries information at vg, not vp. Give delay over length L as L/vg. Mention that waveguide dispersion changes N_g; leave full dispersion treatment to Unit 2.
chapters.example: At λ = 1550 nm a fiber has n_eff = 1.46 and group index N_g = 1.48. Take c = 3.00 × 10^8 m/s. Find vp, vg and the pulse delay over 10 km. vp = 3.00 × 10^8/1.46 = 2.05 × 10^8 m/s. vg = 3.00 × 10^8/1.48 = 2.03 × 10^8 m/s. Delay = 10,000 m/(2.03 × 10^8 m/s) = 4.93 × 10^−5 s = 49.3 µs.
chapters.trap: Use group index N_g for pulse delay, not n_eff. Phase velocity is not the speed at which information travels.
chapters.leave: Leave chromatic dispersion, material dispersion and waveguide dispersion to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Integrated optical waveguides confine light in a high-index strip or channel on a chip, using the same total-internal-reflection idea in two dimensions.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this in detail. Compare strip (ridge) and channel (embedded) waveguides. Define core, substrate and cladding indices. Explain 2D confinement and effective index. Give approximate single-mode check V = (2πt/λ)√(n1² − n2²) using core thickness t. Mention applications in photonic integrated circuits and link to Mach–Zehnder modulators in Unit 3.
chapters.example: A strip waveguide has core thickness t = 0.5 µm, width w = 2 µm, n1 = 1.50, n2 = 1.45 and λ = 1.55 µm. Find NA and the approximate V for the thickness direction. NA = √(1.50² − 1.45²) = √(2.25 − 2.1025) = 0.384. V = (2π × 0.5/1.55) × 0.384 = 2.027 × 0.384 = 0.778. V < 2.405 suggests single-mode behaviour in the thickness direction, approximately.
chapters.trap: A channel waveguide is not the same cross-section as a strip waveguide. The fiber V formula is not exact for a 2D integrated waveguide; use it only as an approximate check.
chapters.leave: Leave modulator structures to Unit 3 and leave photonic crystal waveguides to Chapter 1.9.

chapters.idea: A periodic arrangement of dielectric materials creates a photonic band gap: some wavelengths cannot propagate, enabling traps and guides for light.
chapters.depth: Electromagnetic waves in a periodic medium; 1D Bragg stack; period a and average index n_eff; Bragg wavelength λB ≈ 2 n_eff a. Define photonic band gap and omnidirectional reflector. Survey 2D and 3D photonic crystals, line-defect waveguides, microcavities, photonic crystal fiber, negative refraction and self-collimation at block level. Mention plasmonics and metamaterials only as related advanced topics; do not derive them here.
chapters.example: A 1D photonic crystal has period a = 500 nm and average refractive index n_eff = 1.5. Find the first-order band-gap centre. λB = 2 n_eff a = 2 × 1.5 × 500 nm = 1500 nm. The high-reflection band is centred near 1500 nm.
chapters.trap: The band gap is a range of wavelengths, not one exact wavelength. The period a is one full layer pair, not the thickness of a single layer.
chapters.leave: Leave plasmonics, metamaterials and transformation optics to advanced reading outside this unit.
